output.query: Semantic variant primary progressive aphasia svPPA diagnostic criteria Gorno-Tempini 2011

results.finding: Gorno-Tempini 2011 defines svPPA by two obligatory features: (1) impaired confrontation naming and (2) impaired single-word comprehension. Three of four additional features must be present: impaired object knowledge, surface dyslexia or dysgraphia, spared repetition, and spared speech production. Neuroimaging: left-predominant anterior temporal atrophy or hypometabolism. The condition is associated with TDP-43 type C pathology in the majority of sporadic cases.
results.title: Classification of primary progressive aphasia and its variants (Gorno-Tempini et al., Neurology 2011)

results.finding: Primary progressive aphasia variants (svPPA, nfvPPA, lvPPA) are classified as language-variant FTDs. svPPA is distinguished from bvFTD by the absence of early behavioral disinhibition, perseveration, or hyperorality. svPPA is distinct from typical AD: naming and comprehension deficits occur in the context of preserved episodic memory and visuospatial skills early in the disease course.
results.title: Frontotemporal dementia — Lancet review (Bang et al., 2015)

results.finding: FDG-PET identifies anterior temporal hypometabolism in semantic dementia with high sensitivity. Temporoparietal and posterior cingulate hypometabolism is characteristic of AD; anterior temporal predominant hypometabolism with posterior cingulate sparing distinguishes svPPA from AD.
results.title: FDG-PET improves accuracy in distinguishing FTD and AD (Foster et al., Brain 2007)

findings.finding: Confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test — BNT): 26/60 (1st percentile — severely impaired). Errors are anomic circumlocutions ('the thing for cutting,' 'that bird'). No phonemic cueing benefit. No semantic benefit on verbal definitions when the name is provided.

Single-word comprehension (Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test — PPVT): 68th percentile for 8-year-olds — severely impaired for a 65-year-old with a graduate-level education. Cannot reliably point to pictured objects when the examiner speaks the word aloud ('Show me the comb'; 'Show me the funnel').

Category fluency (animals in 60 seconds): 6 items — severely impaired (mean for age >18 items). Letter fluency (F-words in 60 seconds): 8 items — low-normal for age. Category fluency more impaired than letter fluency — reverse of the typical AD pattern.

Surface dyslexia: reads regular words accurately but makes regularisation errors on irregularly spelled words. Reads 'colonel' as 'col-on-el', 'yacht' as 'yatch', 'pint' as 'pint' (correct), 'have' as 'hayve', 'subtle' as 'sub-tul' — 8 of 15 irregular words misread (53% error rate). Regular words: 14/15 correct.

Repetition: Repeats single words accurately. Sentence repetition intact ('No ifs, ands, or buts' — correct; 'The lawyer's closing argument convinced him' — correct). Digit span: forward 7, backward 5 (normal).
Grammar and syntax: Connected speech is fluent, effortless, and grammatically correct. Reading of grammatically complex sentences (syntactic comprehension) intact.

Episodic memory (Hopkins Verbal Learning Test — HVLT-R): Immediate recall 9/12 across 3 trials (45th percentile — low-average but not severely impaired). Delayed recall 7/12 (35th percentile). Recognition 11/12 (60th percentile — largely preserved). Free recall mildly reduced; recognition substantially intact.
Visuospatial (Rey-O Complex Figure copy): 32/36 (60th percentile — preserved). Block design: 50th percentile.
Executive function (DKEFS Trails condition 4 — switching): 35th percentile (average). Color-Word Inhibition: 40th percentile. Executive function grossly preserved.
Behavioral rating scales (informant — wife): Frontal Behavioral Inventory (FBI) total score: 4/72 — not elevated. No disinhibition, no perseveration, no hyperorality identified by informant rating.

output.impression: Neuropsychological profile: severely impaired confrontation naming (BNT 26/60, 1st percentile), profoundly impaired single-word comprehension (PPVT score at 8-year-old equivalent), and surface dyslexia (53% error rate on irregular words), occurring in the context of preserved speech fluency, intact repetition, preserved grammar, and relatively preserved episodic memory recognition. Category fluency is more impaired than letter fluency. Executive function and visuospatial processing are grossly preserved. Behavioural rating scales show no frontal-behavioral syndrome. Pattern indicates a selective anterior-temporal-network semantic-knowledge deficit

findings.finding: Marked hypometabolism involving the left temporal pole and anterior fusiform/inferior temporal gyrus. FDG uptake 38% below cerebellar reference in the temporal pole; 28% reduction in the anterior fusiform gyrus. This is the dominant metabolic abnormality.
Mild hypometabolism of the right temporal pole (14% reduction vs cerebellar reference). Substantially less severe than the left.
Mildly reduced FDG uptake in Broca-adjacent territory (12% reduction) — less prominent than the temporal changes.
Posterior cingulate cortex, precuneus, and parietal association cortex show preserved FDG uptake bilaterally. No temporoparietal hypometabolism.
FDG uptake in bilateral hippocampi preserved and symmetric — no mesial temporal hypometabolism.
Bilateral prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortices show preserved FDG uptake. No frontal hypometabolism.

output.impression: Marked left-predominant anterior temporal hypometabolism involving the temporal pole and anterior fusiform cortex. Right anterior temporal pole mildly involved. Posterior cingulate, precuneus, and parietal cortex metabolism preserved. Frontal and hippocampal metabolism preserved. The distribution pattern is asymmetric left anterior temporal predominant

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no evidence of benefit in svPPA and may worsen agitation; these are Alzheimer-specific agents.
Do not start memantine: no evidence of benefit in FTD variants including svPPA.

Avoid empirical antiviral therapy (aciclovir) for suspected HSV encephalitis in the absence of encephalopathy, fever, or imaging/CSF evidence of active infection — the atrophy pattern and clinical course are inconsistent with active encephalitis.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line symptomatic management; reserve for refractory behavioral agitation with specialist oversight.
required_recommendations: Apply Gorno-Tempini 2011 svPPA criteria explicitly: confirm both obligatory features (impaired confrontation naming AND impaired single-word comprehension) and at least 3 of 4 supportive features.

Distinguish semantic memory loss (word and object knowledge deficit) from episodic amnesia: this patient loses the meanings of words and objects, not memories of personal events — a critical distinction from Alzheimer disease.
Confirm MRI findings do not show encephalomalacia, hemosiderin, or T2 signal abnormality in temporal lobes before attributing atrophy to prior encephalitis.
Refer to speech-language therapy for compensatory communication strategies and caregiver counseling.
Counsel the patient and family that behavioural changes may emerge later in the disease course as atrophy extends; monitoring is required.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in svPPA/FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course raises concern for prion disease or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of a language-variant FTD; no cardiac indication in this presentation.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative progressive aphasia syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to svPPA and not indicated absent syncope, palpitations, or stroke workup.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution needed to characterise anterior temporal lobar atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study for PPA workup.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; not indicated in svPPA, which has no parkinsonism, tremor, or features of PD/DLB/atypical parkinsonism.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine PPA or FTD diagnostic pathway.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in a neurodegenerative language syndrome.

differential.key_features: Family frames deficits as 'memory problem'; MoCA word recall points mildly reduced — but confrontation naming failure, single-word comprehension loss, surface dyslexia, and preserved episodic recognition argue against amnestic AD.
nfvPPA requires agrammatism and/or effortful speech; speech here is fluent, effortless, and grammatically intact — incompatible with nfvPPA.

MRI shows no encephalomalacia, no T2/FLAIR signal abnormality, no hemosiderin deposits in temporal structures — findings that would be expected with prior HSV encephalitis; wife's report of prior MRI 'asymmetry' is consistent with early svPPA, not a sequela.

differential.diagnosis: Semantic dementia with predominant behavioral change (bvFTD overlap)
differential.key_features: FBI score 4/72 — no frontal behavioral syndrome; preserved social awareness and ADLs; svPPA is the correct primary syndromic classification at this stage.
lvPPA requires impaired sentence repetition and word-retrieval pauses in sentences; repetition is intact and the deficit is semantic (word meaning) not phonological — excludes lvPPA.

key_clinical_evidence: The deficit is semantic (loss of word and object meanings), not episodic (loss of autobiographical events) — the family's framing of a 'memory problem' anchors toward amnestic Alzheimer disease, but the preserved event recall and impaired word comprehension identify this as a semantic variant.

MRI shows left anterior temporal knife-edge atrophy without encephalomalacia, T2 signal change, or hemosiderin — features that would be required to support prior HSV encephalitis; the wife's report of an 'asymmetry' three years ago is consistent with early svPPA, not an encephalitis sequela.

Surface dyslexia (regularisation errors on irregular words such as 'colonel' and 'yacht') is a reliable and specific sign of semantic knowledge loss, supporting svPPA over other PPA variants and over AD.
Category fluency more impaired than letter fluency (reverse of the typical AD pattern) reflects degradation of semantic knowledge networks rather than retrieval failure.

FDG-PET showing anterior temporal hypometabolism with spared posterior cingulate and precuneus directly excludes the Alzheimer metabolic signature and confirms the anterior temporal predominant pattern of svPPA.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. P is a 65-year-old right-handed retired pharmacist of South Asian background, brought to the cognitive neurology clinic by his wife of 38 years, who is the primary historian. She describes a gradual and progressive deterioration over approximately 24 months that she frames as a 'memory problem,' but on careful questioning the nature of the deficit is specific to words and their meanings rather than episodic memory. Mr. P began having difficulty recalling the names of common objects roughly two years ago — at first dismissed as normal aging. His wife noticed that he could not name objects in the kitchen ('the thing for boiling water'), could not recall the names of foods he had eaten for decades, and began referring to plants, animals, and people in photographs by category ('that animal' or 'that person') rather than by name. As a retired pharmacist with 35 years of professional experience, he had previously known the names and mechanisms of hundreds of medications — his wife reports that he can no longer recognize the names of common drugs and does not know what 'ibuprofen' or 'aspirin' means, though he recalls taking tablets for blood pressure. He has also developed difficulty reading irregular English words: he sounds out 'colonel' letter-by-letter and misreads 'yacht' as 'yatch' (surface dyslexia). He remains fully fluent in connected speech — sentences are grammatically correct, effortlessly produced, and his repetition of sentences and digits is intact. Crucially, his wife notes that his memory for events is essentially preserved: he recalls their recent anniversary trip to Vancouver in detail, correctly identifies family members, and accurately recounts the day's events. He has no difficulty with daily routines, handles his medications independently (though he no longer knows their names), manages household finances, and drives without incident. There is no personality change, no disinhibition, no compulsive behaviors, no dietary changes, and no social withdrawal. He has not had seizures, falls, hallucinations, or incontinence. His primary care physician attributed the symptoms to 'normal aging and possible early Alzheimer's' and referred him to cognitive neurology. His wife adds that three years ago, shortly before retirement, an MRI was performed at an outside hospital for a headache workup; she recalls being told 'there was some asymmetry on the left side' but no action was taken. She wonders whether that asymmetry might represent damage from an old brain infection.

neurological_exam.additional: Speech is fluent, effortless, and grammatically intact — no agrammatism, no apraxia of speech, no paraphasias during connected speech. However, word-finding pauses are prominent in conversational speech; he frequently substitutes circumlocutions for specific nouns ('the thing you write with' for pen). Behavioral inventory (informant, wife): no disinhibition, no perseverative behaviors, no hyperorality, no impulsivity, no personality change. Personal hygiene, household finances, and instrumental ADLs are intact. Wife's primary concern is that 'he forgets the names of things — even common objects — and he can no longer read some words he used to know perfectly.'
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact finger-nose and heel-shin bilaterally. Normal rapid alternating movements.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. Extraocular movements intact, no nystagmus, no saccadic pursuits. Face symmetric. Palate elevation intact. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal cadence, stride length, and arm swing. No parkinsonian features. Tandem gait intact.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and cooperative. Well-groomed. Affect appropriate but mildly flat. MoCA 23/30: loses points on naming (0/3 — unable to name rhinoceros, camel, or lion despite recognising these as animals; says 'that big African one' for lion), verbal fluency (0/1 — produces only 4 F-words in 1 minute), and one delayed-recall item (4/5). Executive trails, cube copy, and clock drawing are intact. Digit span: forward 6, backward 4 (normal). Repeats 'no ifs, ands, or buts' correctly. Reading: attempts to read 'Colonel' as 'col-on-el' (sounding out individual letters — surface dyslexia sign). When shown a picture of a stethoscope, he says 'that thing doctors use' rather than naming it. Comprehension of single words severely impaired: cannot identify a comb, a funnel, or a screwdriver by name when examiner says the word and patient must point to the picture.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone throughout. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No tremor. No rigidity. No bradykinesia. No alien limb. No myoclonus.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ symmetric throughout. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffman sign. No grasp reflex. No palmomental reflex.
